title: Boundaries Do Not Mean Growing Apart
deck: Boundaries protect not distance, but the continued presence of two people who can judge and change within a relationship.
body: People often begin to fear boundaries once a relationship grows close.
“Why can’t you tell me about this?”
“Why do you have to decide for yourself?”
“Do we still need to draw such clear lines between us?”
Behind these questions lies a very natural expectation: once two people are close enough, what originally belonged to “you” and “me” should gradually become “ours.”
Time can be shared, space can be shared, and so can plans and responsibilities. A relationship does indeed allow two people’s lives to enter into one another.
But entering into one another’s lives does not mean disappearing into them.
What boundaries truly protect is more than private space. They protect the continued presence of two people in a relationship.

If someone cannot retain their own judgment, have feelings they need not explain immediately, or spend time alone with certain matters, the relationship may seem very close. Yet it becomes harder and harder to tell who is choosing, who is agreeing, and who is changing.
Closeness without boundaries may eventually leave only one voice.

This need not come from the stronger person openly issuing orders. It can also happen gradually in daily life. Someone gets used to checking the other person’s reaction before knowing whether they may like something; before a plan has even taken shape, it is revised into something the other person can easily accept; a disagreement is withdrawn before it can be spoken, for fear of damaging intimacy.
On the surface there is no conflict, yet differences have never truly entered the relationship.
This kind of “we” is stable because one person within it is continually making themselves smaller.
Boundaries are not meant to prevent closeness, but to keep closeness meaningful.

Only when someone can say no is their yes more than compliance. Only when they can keep something to themselves is sharing truly sharing. Only when they can step away from a decision is staying a choice.
Two people can encounter one another precisely because they are not the same person.
Boundaries therefore do not mean keeping everything strictly separate.
Some decisions need to be made together in the first place. Shared resources, shared risks, and commitments already made cannot be entirely excluded from discussion by saying, “This is my boundary.”
Boundaries protect a person from being replaced by another, but do not cancel the responsibilities that have genuinely arisen between them.

Someone cannot invoke private space to conceal important facts that would change the other person’s choices, or use independent decision-making as a reason to leave all the shared consequences to others.
A boundary, then, is not a wall that never opens.

It is more like a line both people need to see: here is what I can decide for myself; there is what you can decide; and there are also areas where, because our lives are connected, we need to negotiate together.
This line is not drawn once and for all.

Relationships change, trust grows, and responsibilities change too. Some things that once belonged solely to one person may later need to be handled together; some areas that were once extensively shared may come to need space again.
Mature boundaries are not rigid. They can be explained, discussed with a willingness to listen, and revised.
But revision must come from both people’s genuine responses, not from a presumption that the closer you are, the less right you have to remain yourself.
Sometimes, when someone says, “I need a little space,” they have not stopped loving, nor are they preparing to leave.

They may simply need to hear their own thoughts again without having to respond immediately to another person. Someone who always lives amid the echoes of a relationship may eventually lose track of which wishes are their own and which have formed only to keep the peace.
An appropriate distance can allow them to return with a clearer sense of themselves.
Of course, boundaries can also be used as a means of avoidance.

Someone may suddenly insist on independence when a burden needs to be shared, refuse any explanation when the other person asks reasonable questions, or dress up coldness and disappearing from contact as “respecting space.”
To judge whether a boundary is genuine, we need to consider not only how much it separates, but whether it also acknowledges the other person’s place.

A boundary that protects only my freedom while leaving you to bear all the uncertainty I create is incomplete. A genuine boundary also makes clear what belongs to me, what affects you, and what I am willing to bear for my own choices.
The best relationships are not those in which you and I can no longer be distinguished.

Amid the many things in a shared life, they still allow two people to see, think, and change for themselves. They do not treat differences as evidence of insufficient intimacy or demand that someone disappear as a person to prove their trust.
Boundaries are not a failure of the relationship.
They are what allows a relationship to keep growing closer without turning either person into an extension of the other.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
